### 28.3 Residuals — stated, not hidden

| # | Residual | Bound |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| **M7-R-01** | A runtime-role actor holding the CCA-private participant credential can call a participant function directly and thereby write an M7 fact **without** consent evaluation. The assignment lock, session validation, coherence checks and generation stamping still apply | The same boundary A1 and A2 already accept for their own consent-conditioned writes (A2 §4.1; CCA §40.2, §45). Strengthening it in the database would require a second consent algorithm, which CCA-SEM forbids; §18.3.1 strengthens only the topology (CS-1…CS-5) and its verification. Made visible by test **T-23**; mitigated by credential scoping (IMP-03) |
| **M7-R-02** | Participant identity rests ultimately on authentication; an actor holding **both** the issuer credential and the participant credential can mint a session for any participant | FINAL §28 and A1 §12 put full authentication outside scope. Two-credential separation is required (IMP-03) and every issuance is attributed (`issuedBy`) |
| **M7-R-03** | Owner-class actors can alter data, guards, functions, ACLs and control-plane rows, and can re-register an expectation set to match what they changed | JBA §19.4 and PR-5: governance, not technical enforcement. The exact-set verifier makes such changes **detectable** to an unmodified verifier holding the reviewed manifest — which is all BI-32 permits claiming — and the manifest's own digest is published outside the database (§24.2) |
| **M7-R-04** | A storage worker could report an observation, or an `ABSENT_CONFIRMED` attempt, that does not match reality on the backend it declares | The worker is a trusted capability by construction. SI-3 removes the **accidental** false confirmation (wrong backend after a rotation) entirely — that class is now a DB error, not a silent success — but a deliberately lying worker remains outside enforcement. Audit sweeps (T-63, T-64) detect divergence after the fact, and the DB verifies mismatch claims (M7-I61) |
| **M7-R-05** | Backups, provider replicas and WAL may retain bytes or rows after a lawful deletion | Outside M7's technical boundary; an operational retention obligation (PR-5 analogue). M7 never reconstructs purged residue (M7-I57) |
| **M7-R-06** | A `PRESIGNED_PUT` URL cannot be revoked before its ≤ 300 s expiry | Bounded to the staging zone of one backend, which can never become canonical evidence (M7-I35) |
| **M7-R-07** | Evidence written to a backend that must later be decommissioned cannot be moved; it can only be drained (deleted) or the backend kept alive | Deliberate: a migration path is exactly where `M7V11-AUD-01`'s false-proof risk reappears. V1.1 refuses to grant one (§11.4, M7-I92) and leaves it to a future artifact with its own verification suite |
| **M7-R-08** | One extra canonical object is written, and later deleted, for every lease expiry on an upload intent | The accepted cost of external generation fencing (§11.6.3). Bounded by `finalizeWindow / workerLease` per intent (CB-17, T-123) |
| **M7-R-09** | The write fence of §11.7 rests on facts PostgreSQL cannot observe: that no M7 credential can create objects under `<evidencePrefix>` (XC-1), that the provider rejects a create for a key the capability does not name (SP-10), and that the provider bounds in-flight write visibility by the declared `W` (SP-9) | All are **deployment conditions with adversarial cases**, not assumptions: XC-1 by T-138b, SP-10 by T-167, `W` by T-142, all against the real provider (IMP-15, IMP-16). The database proves the scheduling half — that no absence proof is executable before the fence (M7-I109) — and the envelope half (M7-I118), and this document claims nothing further. A deployment that cannot demonstrate all three has **not** closed `M7V11R2-AUD-01` |
| **M7-R-12** | **The signer's fidelity is deployment capability topology, not database or provider enforcement.** A signer module that ignored the envelope `m7.x_mint_generation_capability_v1` returned and signed something wider — a prefix, another key, a later expiry — would falsify the XF-THEOREM's step (1). No database object and no provider ACL prevents it where `envelopeEnforcement = SIGNER_TOPOLOGY` | Bounded and named rather than absorbed. The database proves everything around it: one function returns an envelope, its signature admits no envelope component (SD-13, T-135), its grantee set is exactly one role, that role's EXECUTE set has cardinality 1, the worker role is excluded, no role holds both (IA-14, T-171b (i)–(iii)). The remaining claim is **M7-I119**, class **E-E**, published in the manifest as `deployment.capabilitySigner` (MA-15) and verified only by dependency closure (T-171b (iv), IMP-18). Where the provider's own IAM can pin the envelope, the deployment declares `PROVIDER_IAM` and this residual drops to M7-R-09's kind (**E-D**). **This residual is the honest remainder of `M7V11R3-AUD-01` and is stated here rather than in a footnote, because the theorem depends on it** |
| **M7-R-13** | Retirement safety rests on **every** transaction that creates a drain obligation or mints external write authority taking the liveness lock (BL-2), and on no other transaction being able to move a row into a drain class (BL-9). A future function that inserts an intent, generation, artifact, `PENDING` outbox row or mint without the lock, or a future guard transition that re-opens an obligation, would break the BL-THEOREM's step (c) or (d) | Bounded by making the set a **derivation** rather than a list: §11.10.4 states the rule; `database.backendLivenessFunctions[]` publishes its result (MA-16); **T-180** recomputes the rule from the source and compares it with the helper call sites, §11.10.4 and the manifest in both directions, checks P2 placement, and checks BL-9 against the guard transition tables; a violation is write-disabling (IMP-19). Round 3's version of this residual rested on a syntactic predicate its own bodies contradicted |
| **M7-R-14** | LG-THEOREM rests on PostgreSQL's row-lock **conflict matrix**, on the implicit lock modes of PG-2 (foreign keys, updates, deletes, unique insertions) and on PG-3's property that a failed `NOWAIT` leaves no waiting request. A server version that changed any of them could admit a cycle the theorem excludes. *Round 4's version of this residual also rested on a no-queueing clause that was false (`M7V11R5-AUD-01`); that dependency is removed* | Stated as premises and tested: T-188 (ii)–(vii) on the deployed major version (IMP-21), with (i) recording — not demanding — whether a compatible request queues behind an incompatible waiter, since the conservative PG-1 admits both; `lock_timeout` bounds every wait a work transaction performs; the deadlock detector remains a backstop that the suite treats as a failure |
| **M7-R-15** | A row mechanism refuses instead of waiting when any target row is locked (LG-5), so an assignment under continuous activity can delay an authorized erasure | Deliberate: a waiting row mechanism is the one transaction that could otherwise hold the assignment while waiting on half of M7. The refusal is typed (`ROW_MECHANISM_TARGET_BUSY`), the scheduler retries, and the execution's hard deadline and SLA views (§15.11.4) surface any delay rather than hiding it |
| **M7-R-16** | A storage retirement **never waits** (LG-10): under continuous C/M work on its backend — credential rotation of the active backend under sustained load being the realistic case — every attempt can meet a liveness holder and raise `M7014` until the governed retry budget is exhausted | Deliberate: the alternative is a waiting exclusive request, which is the queue head `M7V11R5-AUD-01` shows can close a cycle, or a mechanism that sacrifices work for retirement, which RR-4 forbids. Safety is unaffected — an unretired backend strands nothing — and the delay is visible (`RETIREMENT_NOT_ACHIEVED`). Operators schedule retirement in a low-traffic window or after RT-3 has moved new work away (RR-7); T-193 |
| **M7-R-17** | The affected-row count of a purge with `retainDeletionHistory = false` exists only in the return value of the call that performed it; if that response is lost, the count is unrecoverable, and a retry cannot tell a completed residue-free purge from an execution id that never existed (`EXECUTION_ABSENT`) | Deliberate and required by JBA §16.6.1 Case 2: any stored count, marker or distinguishable response would be residue. The purge's effect is not lost — the rows are gone, and a retry deletes nothing and recreates nothing (RM-4…RM-6, CB-24, T-61 (d), (e)) |
| **M7-R-10** | An actor holding the **object-store credentials themselves** (provider console, leaked deployment secret) can write a canonical key after its deletion was confirmed | Outside M7's threat boundary, and distinct from M7-R-03 (which concerns database owner-class actors). With fencing in force such a write can no longer be a tolerated race, so `CANONICAL_OBJECT_PRESENT_AFTER_DELETION` becomes an unambiguous integrity alarm (§17.4): the object is re-enqueued for deletion, the completion record is **not** revoked, and the finding stands permanently beside it |
| **M7-R-11** | `G` (the write-grant TTL) is the worker's real budget for the canonical write, and XF-DL-1 caps `G + W + Λ` at `workerLease` (≤ 120 s). A slow provider or a large image can therefore exhaust `G` and force a reclaim | Deliberate and bounded: the alternative is a longer-lived write capability, which is precisely what `M7V11R2-AUD-01` rejects. The cost is the same bounded extra object as M7-R-08, and a manifest whose parameters cannot satisfy XF-DL-1 is refused at activation rather than run (M7-I110) |

Words such as READY, COMPLETE or PASS anywhere in this document describe **author-side** readiness only. Nothing here accepts this candidate, and nothing here authorizes implementation. Those decisions belong to an independent auditor and to the protected integration process.

**Two closure claims in this document are explicitly conditional, and they are conditional on different things.** `M7V11R2-AUD-01` / `M7V11R3-AUD-01` is a claim about what an external object store will refuse **and** about what an external signer will sign. The database half — envelope derivation, mint refusal, the ACL topology — is enforced here. The **provider** half (XC-1, SP-9, SP-10) is an ACL and provider fact PostgreSQL cannot observe: §26.1 states it for invariant **M7-I107**, §28.3 records it as residual **M7-R-09**, and §25.18 makes T-138b, T-142 and T-167 real-provider cases whose pass condition is a provider rejection. The **signer** half (XC-5, XC-6) is deployment capability topology that neither PostgreSQL nor a provider ACL settles: it is invariant **M7-I119**, class **E-E**, residual **M7-R-12**, prerequisite **IMP-18**, and case **T-171b**. §27.5 states both in the finding's own Status cell. The author does **not** report that finding as closed on database evidence alone, and an auditor should not accept it on that basis either.

**Round-4 findings are not reported as accepted either.** The round-4 candidate `c1cbe6e7` received `REQUIRES PATCH (ROUND 5)`. §27.7.1 records, per round-4 repair, how it interacts with this round; none of its six closure claims, and neither of the two round-5 closures in §27.7, is described as independently accepted.

**Round-3 findings are not reported as accepted either.** The round-3 candidate `bf65f309` received `REQUIRES PATCH (ROUND 4)`. §27.6.1 records, per round-3 repair, whether it is preserved, corrected or superseded here; no round-3 closure claim is described as independently accepted, and none of the six round-4 closures in §27.6 is either.

**Round-2 findings are not reported as accepted.** The round-2 candidate `20afa33c` received the verdict `REQUIRES PATCH (ROUND 3)` and was **not accepted**, so none of its four closure claims was independently accepted. §27.4 records the honest disposition per finding: `M7V11R2-AUD-01` **not closed**, superseded by `M7V11R3-AUD-01`; `M7V11R2-AUD-02` and `M7V11R2-AUD-03` **closed normatively and preserved without regression**; `M7V11R2-AUD-04`'s original single-drain-predicate defect **closed and preserved**, with `M7V11R3-AUD-02` a **new blocker** on the same two functions.

## A.0.R5 Round 5 — the two binding findings of the fifth independent audit

The round-4 candidate `c1cbe6e7` received `REQUIRES PATCH (ROUND 5)`. Its two findings share a shape different from round 4's:

> **Each round-5 finding is a place where a property of the *environment* was stated more strongly than the environment guarantees, and a proof or invariant was then built on the stronger statement.** PG-1 asserted a PostgreSQL queueing behaviour that PostgreSQL deliberately does not provide, and the theorem used it at exactly the edge that closed a cycle. M7-I58 asserted replay idempotency for a family of functions whose weakest member had no replay check at all, and whose residue-prohibited member cannot, by law, keep what a replay would need.
>
> The corresponding discipline, applied throughout this revision: **state the weakest premise that is certainly true, prove against that, and where the proof then fails, change the design rather than strengthen the premise.** Lemma Q, table C, table LV and the RM table of §15.7.1 are the templates.

## A.0.R4 Round 4 — the six binding findings of the fourth independent audit

The round-3 candidate `bf65f309` received `REQUIRES PATCH (ROUND 4)`. Its findings share one shape, and it is the shape an auditor should look for in this revision too:

> **Each round-4 finding is a place where an enumeration or a derivation was declared complete and was not derived from the thing it enumerates.** The owner table was declared complete and omitted an owner. The lock order was declared universal and was not read off the function bodies. The liveness set was defined by a textual predicate and did not match the bodies it named. The mint's provenance was declared bound and was bound twice, independently. The expiry check was declared authoritative and read the clock at the wrong time. The counts were declared derived and the subtotals were not.
>
> The corresponding discipline, applied throughout this revision: **derive every set and every order from the SQL first, publish the derivation, and make a test recompute it.** §11.10.4's rule, §16.2.6's matrix, §16.2.7's wait table and §19.14.1's rules are the templates.

## A.0 Round 3 — the four binding findings of the third independent audit

The round-2 candidate `20afa33c` received `REQUIRES PATCH (ROUND 3)`. Four more findings, again treated as **architecture** requirements rather than wording. Their common shape is different from round 2's and is worth naming, because it is what an auditor should look for next:

> **Each round-3 finding is a place where a mechanism was credited with enforcing something it structurally cannot.** A `PRIMARY KEY` over a row was credited with bounding the number of *signatures produced outside the database*. A `FOR UPDATE` taken by one party was credited with *serializing a party that never takes it*. One identifier was credited with carrying *two meanings*. A count edited in two places was credited with being *the count everywhere*. In every case the object cited exists and does what it does; the claim attached to it was larger than the object.
>
> The corresponding discipline, applied throughout this revision: **name the enforcing layer for every claim, and when the layer cannot reach the claim, either move the claim to something the layer can enforce (the envelope instead of the token count; a two-sided lock instead of a one-sided one) or classify the gap honestly and test it (E-E, M7-I119, T-171b).** §11.7.4 is the template.

## A.0.1 Round 2 — the four findings of the second audit

Round 1 repaired seven findings; the independent verdict `REQUIRES PATCH (ROUND 2)` found four more. Each was again treated as an **architecture** requirement. **Round 3's verdict on these is in §27.4 and is not "all four accepted":** two are closed normatively and preserved here, one is partially closed with a new blocker, and one was not closed at all. The common shape of all four is worth naming:

> **Each round-2 finding is a place where a mechanism was correct about the database and silent about the world.** A per-generation key fenced *adoption* but not *creation*. A persisted `deadlinePolicyVersion` fixed the *deadline* but not the *runtime that must meet it*. A copied `storageProfileId` recorded an *identity* that had stopped being the *actor*. Two spellings of "drained" agreed on the *name* and not on the *predicate*. In every case the DDL was internally consistent and the claim it supported was false.

## A.2 Adversarial self-review of the repairs

Defects found in the **new** architecture during self-review, and fixed before the candidate commit:

| # | Defect found in the repair itself | Fix |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 1 | The first draft of the storage binding stored only `storageProfileId`, forcing every routing check to join through `m7_storage_profile`. That is still a single hop, but it made composite foreign keys impossible, so *nothing at the constraint level* prevented an attempt row from naming a foreign backend | `backendSha256` is **denormalized onto every storage-bearing row** and trigger-verified, which enables `m7_storage_effect_attempt(outboxId, executingBackendSha256) → m7_storage_outbox(id, backendSha256)`. The routing guarantee is now a foreign key, not only a function check |
| 2 | Per-generation keys initially reused the intent's single 32-hex suffix with the epoch appended. A predictable key lets a stale worker write a *future* epoch's object before that epoch is claimed | each generation gets its **own** fresh `gen_random_uuid()`-derived suffix, allocated inside the claim transaction, so no future key is guessable or writable |
| 3 | The first `t_outbox_coherence` allowed a canonical delete for any generation row, including the **live** one — which would delete bytes under a working worker | the GF-7 branch now refuses a delete for the accepted generation of a live intent and for the current epoch of a `PROCESSING` intent (T-122 asserts `OWNED` for both) |
| 4 | The CB-04 recovery inherited from the previous candidate ("reclaim finds the object and reads it back") is *exactly* the adoption AUD-02 forbids; it survived into an early draft of §17.3 | CB-04 and CB-05 were **rewritten**: a reclaim re-reads staging and writes its own generation. The old recovery text is gone, and T-69 asserts the new behaviour including the sweep of the crashed generation |
| 5 | Making `budgetSatisfied = false` a *refusal* in `t_deletion_execution_verify` seemed safer, but it would block deletion of already-late data — retaining bytes to protect a metric | the trigger derives and records the flag and **still creates the execution**; the row surfaces in `v_deletion_sla_critical` (T-129b asserts exactly this) |
| 6 | `rawDeleteScheduleAfterWithdrawal` was initially omitted (withdrawal "schedules immediately"), which left DL-1 un-instantiated for that basis and made `L` unaccounted | all three bases carry the full triple, with `S ≥ 0` permitted for withdrawal and authorized deletion, and DL-1 enforced for each |
| 7 | Removing the vocabulary from the request hash creates an ambiguity if a `merchantRef` ever denotes different merchants in different vocabulary versions | **RP-5** makes ref stability normative, §13.4 states it, and **MA-4** makes a future rotation prove it |
| 8 | An early expectation-set design keyed functions by `proname`, which cannot distinguish overloads and would silently accept an added overload | expectations are keyed by `oid::regprocedure::text`, i.e. the full argument signature; an added overload is `FN-EXTRA` (T-135) |
| 9 | `i_catalog_violations()` originally took no argument and read "the active manifest" itself, which meant the verifier's own answer depended on mutable state it was supposed to be checking | it now takes `p_manifest_version`; `w_verify_control_plane_catalog_v1` resolves it **after** proving the caller's digest matches, and the final install `DO` block passes the version it just activated |
| 10 | `c_activate_manifest_v1` initially allowed activation before any expectation set existed, which would leave the verifier vacuously satisfied | activation now refuses a manifest with no loaded expectation set (T-116) |
| 11 | The one-open-effect index was still keyed `(effectKind, objectKey)`, so the *same* key on two backends collided — reusing one backend's effect row to "confirm" the other's | re-keyed to `(effectKind, backendSha256, objectKey)`; the reconciliation-finding uniqueness likewise gained `backendSha256` |
| 12 | Zone CHECKs still hard-coded `m7/staging/` and `m7/evidence/`, re-coupling keys to one literal backend | CHECKs now pin only row-local shape; the **prefix** is verified against the bound backend by `t_upload_intent_coherence`, `t_generation_coherence`, `t_outbox_coherence` and `t_reconciliation_finding_coherence` |
| 13 | `w_record_validated_observation_v1` accepted any `encoderVersion` string, so a profile rotation could not be distinguished in the record | the column is `encoderGeneration` and the function requires it to equal the **executing profile's** pinned value (T-118) |
| 14 | The purge did not delete `m7_canonical_generation` rows, so a purged assignment left orphan generation rows referencing deleted intents | step (2) of `w_execute_row_purge_v1` deletes generations before intents; control-plane identity rows remain explicitly non-purgeable (T-59, T-60) |
| 15 | `m7_evidence_upload_intent`'s `acceptedLeaseEpoch` CHECK initially forced NULL outside `VALIDATED`/`CONSUMED`, which would erase the accepted-generation record on U9 expiry | the CHECK permits a retained value in the three terminal states, and the guard makes the column write-once under U5 only |

### A.2.1 Defects found in the **round-2** repairs during self-review

| # | Defect found in the repair itself | Fix |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 16 | The first fencing draft set `writeFenceAt = grantExpiresAt` only, i.e. it assumed a request cannot complete after its signature expires. That is false for every provider that validates expiry at request **acceptance**, which is the normal behaviour — so a slow `PUT` accepted one millisecond before expiry could still land after the fence | `W` (`providerWriteCompletionWindow`) was introduced as an explicit SP-9 bound and added to the arithmetic, to `backendSha256`, to the manifest and to T-142. The round-2 brief asked for exactly this case and the first draft would have failed it |
| 17 | `W` was first placed on the storage **profile**, which would have let a credential rotation silently lower it under fences already computed from the old value | `W` is a **backend** identity field and is inside `i_backend_digest` (XF-10), so changing it produces a different backend and no existing fence is re-parameterised (T-143b) |
| 18 | XF-DL-1 (`G + W + Λ ≤ workerLease`) was first written as a table CHECK, which is impossible: `G` and `Λ` live on the policy and `W` on the backend | the single-table half became `m7_retention_policy_grant_ttl_ck`; the full relation is verified in `c_activate_manifest_v1` (the one place binding exactly one policy and one backend) and re-verified per allocation in `w_claim_upload_intent_v1` and `t_generation_coherence`, raising `M7012` |
| 19 | The staging zone was initially left unfenced — only canonical keys were. A participant `PUT` accepted just before `uploadExpiresAt` could therefore land **after** a staging `DELETE` + `HEAD` had confirmed absence, reproducing the same defect one zone over | `stagingWriteFenceAt` was added to the intent, derived and trigger-verified, and every staging enqueue (U5, U6, U7, U9, reconciliation) now uses it instead of `uploadExpiresAt` |
| 20 | `m7.i_enqueue_delete` was first left to trust its `p_not_before` argument, with the fence check only in the coherence trigger. A future caller passing an early value would then get a confusing trigger error instead of correct behaviour | the helper itself raises `notBefore` to `m7.i_object_write_fence(...)`, and the trigger re-checks. Callers that also pass the fence explicitly (the sweep, U5) are redundant on purpose |
| 21 | The first §11.9 predicate had five classes and still permitted retiring a backend that held a superseded generation object nobody had ever swept — so §11.1.5's sentence *"every byte M7 ever wrote there is confirmed absent"* was still false, in a narrower way | classes **6 and 7** were added: every canonical key and every staging key on the backend must have a `CONFIRMED` `DELETE_OBJECT` effect. This is the class the original wording implied and no implementation checked |
| 22 | Classes 6 and 7 broke under `ROW_PURGE`: a purge removed outbox rows while leaving generations, so a purged assignment made its backend permanently undrainable | `w_execute_row_purge_v1` removes generations, grants, requeue records and effect rows in the same transaction, so purged rows contribute to neither side of the predicate. The interaction is stated in §11.9.2 rather than left to be rediscovered |
| 23 | The first DL-5 draft carried `boundPolicyVersion` and validated it only in `t_outbox_coherence`. A trigger is the weakest place to hold a binding that three different enqueue paths write | three **composite foreign keys** were added (`(deletionExecutionId, boundPolicyVersion)`, `(uploadIntentId, boundPolicyVersion)`, `(reconciliationFindingId, boundPolicyVersion)`) with the supporting UNIQUEs, so a wrong bound policy is `23503`. `MATCH SIMPLE` makes each active exactly for its own family, and `_binding_ck` makes the three exhaustive |
| 24 | `w_lease_outbox_v1` first resolved the bound policy **once per call**, which is wrong the moment one batch spans two policies — precisely the situation a rotation creates | the policy is resolved **per row inside the loop** (T-151's batch deliberately mixes two policies) |
| 25 | The requeue fix first kept a separate `attemptsInWindow` counter alongside `attempts`, which made the lifetime count ambiguous and the guard hard to state | a single monotone `attempts` plus `attemptBudgetBase`; the guard forbids either moving backwards, so a reset is `restrict_violation` rather than a value the trigger has to interpret |
| 26 | An early draft let `w_requeue_failed_effect_v1` clear an existing `m7_deletion_sla_failure` row when the effect later succeeded — which is exactly the laundering the finding objects to | SLA failures are append-only and survive completion; instead the **completion** records `withinCompletionBudget = false`, and `v_deletion_sla_critical` reports both |
| 27 | Making the observation's `encoderGeneration` equal to the *currently live* profile's value was the obvious fix for R2-AUD-02 and is wrong: after a second rotation the historical row would no longer validate | it is bound to the **generation's own executing profile** by the composite FK `(executingProfileId, encoderGeneration)`, which is a fact about that generation and never about the present |
| 28 | Renaming the intent's column to `issuanceProfileId` initially left `t_generation_coherence` requiring generation-profile = intent-profile, so the rename alone would have changed nothing | the equality is **deleted**, EP-2 states that it must not exist, and T-145 asserts that a generation with a different executing profile commits without objection |
| 29 | `m7_storage_observation.encoderGeneration` is NULL after redaction, which would have made a plain composite FK unsatisfiable for redacted rows | `MATCH SIMPLE` semantics leave the FK unenforced exactly when the column is NULL, i.e. exactly after redaction, which is the only legitimate state without an encoder. Stated in the DDL comment so it is not read as an oversight |
| 30 | `c_retire_storage_profile_v1` originally evaluated the drain predicate without locking the backend, leaving a window in which a new intent could be issued between the check and the retirement | it takes `FOR UPDATE` on the backend row inside the class-0 rotation transaction. **This fix was incomplete and its accompanying claim was wrong**, which is `M7V11R3-AUD-02`: a lock taken by one party serializes nothing, and `m7.p_begin_evidence_upload_v1` never took it. See A.2.2 #31 |

### A.2.2 Defects found in the **round-3** repairs during self-review

| # | Defect found in the repair itself | Fix |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 31 | The round-2 fix for A.2 #30 added `FOR UPDATE` on the backend row to the **retirement** side only, and RC-19 then asserted that this serialized issuance and enqueueing. It does not: serialization requires both parties to take the lock, and SO-2 took nothing. Self-review had accepted the sentence because the *lock* was real; the *claim about it* was not. **The general lesson is A.0's**: the object existed and the claim attached to it was larger than the object | the lock is now **two-sided** (BL-2/BL-3), every work-creating path is enumerated (§11.10.4) and source-checked (T-180), the property is **proved** (BL-THEOREM) rather than asserted, and five two-session cases in both orders exist so it is falsifiable by execution (T-173…T-176, T-179) |
| 32 | The first round-3 draft tried to preserve the round-2 wording by proving token uniqueness with an added `m7_generation_capability_mint` **`UNIQUE(grantId)`** — one mint row per grant, ever. That is worse than useless: it still cannot observe a token signed without a DB write, and it would make the CB-22 recovery (a lost mint response) unrecoverable, pushing the worker toward exactly the out-of-band reminting the finding is about | the mint table is keyed `UNIQUE(grantId, mintSeq)` and re-minting is **deliberately allowed and deliberately visible**. Safety comes from the *envelope* FK (XF-11), not from a count. T-169 asserts envelope equality across mints; Corollary 4 states why that suffices |
| 33 | The first envelope FK covered only `(grantId, canonicalObjectKey, grantExpiresAt)`. A mint could then name a **different backend** while keeping the key and expiry — which, with two backends sharing an `evidencePrefix` shape, is a real widening | `backendSha256` and `capabilityOperation` were added to both the grant's envelope `UNIQUE` and the mint's composite FK, so the FK covers all four envelope components plus the grant id. The grant also gained its own composite FK to the generation's `(uploadIntentId, leaseEpoch, backendSha256)`, so the envelope's backend cannot drift from the generation's physical home |
| 34 | `m7.i_capability_envelope_digest` at first hashed the whole grant row, including `capabilityMode` and `envelopeEnforcement`. A profile rotation that changed the capability mode would then have changed the *envelope digest* of an existing grant, making T-169's equality assertion fail for a reason that has nothing to do with authorization | the digest covers exactly the four components of XF-GOAL. Mode and enforcement say *how* the envelope is carried and by *which layer*, not what it authorizes; they are recorded on the grant and excluded from the digest, with a DDL comment saying so |
| 35 | An early version of `m7.x_mint_generation_capability_v1` returned a distinct error for an unknown `generationGrantId`, which makes the function an oracle for which grant ids exist | every refusal is the same `M7013 M7_CAPABILITY_REFUSED` with no `DETAIL`, in the same style as the deliberately indistinguishable `28000` of `i_require_session` |
| 36 | The first liveness draft put the `FOR SHARE` in each enqueue **caller**. Six callers reach `m7.i_enqueue_delete`, and a seventh would have been added by any future scheduler with nobody noticing | the lock is taken **inside the helper** (WC-6), so no caller can omit it; and T-180 checks the rule in both directions over the `prosrc` digests, so a future backend-scoped writer that bypasses the helper fails CI and produces `FN-DRIFT` |
| 37 | `m7.i_hold_backend_liveness` first refused a retired backend unconditionally. That makes `w_execute_row_purge_v1` unable to purge rows on a backend that has been retired — i.e. a lawful erasure would be blocked by a storage-lifecycle state, which is the same category of error as J-11 and #5 above (retaining data to protect a mechanism) | `p_allow_retired` exists, is passed at exactly one call site, is documented as WC-15's exception with the reason (a purge only *removes* obligations), and T-180 (iv) asserts it appears nowhere else |
| 38 | Making class 10 a *new table* (`m7_storage_backend_liveness`) was the first design, to avoid overloading a class-0 row. It would have added a table, a PK, a FK and 3 triggers to hold **no data** | the `m7_storage_backend` row is the liveness object. It is immutable apart from the one-way retirement, so a `FOR SHARE` holder never blocks on a value change — only on the retirement, which is precisely the event the lock exists to serialize against. §16.2.2 states the class-0 exception explicitly rather than leaving it to be inferred |
| 39 | The first draft of `c_retire_storage_profile_v1` kept round 2's order — profile `FOR UPDATE`, then backend — while adding the liveness semantics, which inverts the class-0 internal order `backend ≺ profile` and would have been a genuine deadlock edge between two concurrent retirements on one backend | the backend is resolved with an unlocked read and taken `FOR UPDATE` **first**; the profile follows. §11.10.5 step 4 is the argument, and it only works in this order |
| 40 | RT-2 was first written as "refuse a backend that has any profile named by any manifest". That refuses retirement of a backend named by a **historical, rolled-back** manifest forever, making the drain path unreachable after any rollback | RT-2 is scoped to the **active installation only** (`i."retiredAt" IS NULL`), which is the property that actually needs protecting. T-177 rehearses the rotation-then-retire path end to end so the narrowing is exercised, not just asserted |
| 41 | The round-3 count sweep initially "fixed" T-05 by writing `39` as a literal — the same failure mode as `M7V11R3-AUD-04`, one round later | T-05 now names *the §19.10.1 loop list* as its source of truth and §19.14.1 publishes the derivation rule, so the number cannot go stale independently of the thing it counts. The same treatment was applied to `M7-I04`, AUD-10 and T-07 |
| 42 | Re-identifying the races was first done by renumbering `RC-19 → RC-21` and leaving its text. Its text contained the false serialization claim, so renumbering would have preserved the defect under a new identifier | `RC-21` is **rewritten** onto the mechanism actually specified, and `RC-16` — which had the same one-sided phrasing — is amended too. §16.3.1 records which rows were rewritten rather than renumbered, so an auditor can check the distinction |

### A.2.3 Defects found during the round-4 fresh adversarial review

The brief required a fresh review of function bodies against claimed lock order, every liveness caller and non-caller, owner completeness, definer boundaries, the signer envelope proof, every composite-FK provenance claim, the concurrency cases and the inventory. The review found the following in addition to the six audited findings. Items #43–#52 are defects, each fixed in this candidate; #53 and #54 are designs considered for the repairs and rejected, recorded so an auditor can see why they are absent.

| # | Defect found | Fix |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 43 | Five loop functions (`w_expire_upload_intents_v1`, `w_sweep_superseded_generations_v1`, the three schedulers) acquired the class 4/7 row lock of row *n+1* while holding class 10 for row *n*; `w_sweep_superseded_generations_v1` did so with a **waiting** lock | each completes its P1 batch (`SKIP LOCKED`, or ordered waiting locks in the authorized scheduler) before one ordered liveness call (§16.2.6) |
| 44 | `w_execute_row_purge_v1` took class 10 with `PERFORM i_hold_backend_liveness(b, true) FROM (… ORDER BY 1)`, which does not fix the evaluation order of the calls, and then deleted rows in descending and mixed class order with implicit locks | the purge takes no liveness lock at all (NW-6) and pre-locks every target `NOWAIT` in class order (LG-5); `i_hold_backends_liveness` is the only multi-backend acquisition path |
| 45 | `c_register_merchant_vocabulary_v1` inserted `m7_merchant_vocabulary_entry` rows **before** their `m7_merchant_vocabulary` parent, under a `NOT DEFERRABLE` foreign key: every first registration failed `23503`, so no manifest could ever be installed | the parent row is inserted first with the digest computed from the supplied refs, entries second, and the stored-row digest is still recomputed and compared (R-B-14 preserved) |
| 46 | guard transition **O8** required `NEW."attempts" = 0` while the DL-6 guard in the same trigger forbids `attempts` from moving backwards and `w_requeue_failed_effect_v1` keeps it: every requeue of an effect with attempts > 0 raised `restrict_violation`, so DL-6 and T-154 were unexecutable | O8 requires `attempts` unchanged and `attemptBudgetBase = OLD.attempts` |
| 47 | `w_assert_deletion_sla_failures_v1` ordered its unique insertions by `completionBudgetDueAt` alone, so two concurrent runs could insert tied `(executionId, kind)` keys in opposite orders | ordered by `(completionBudgetDueAt, id)` (IW-5 ordered) |
| 48 | round 3's T-107 asserted that no non-listed function blocks behind an assignment lock; five functions (`r_record_erasure_request_v1`, `a_mint_deletion_authorization_v1`, three schedulers) insert rows whose foreign key takes `FOR KEY SHARE` on the assignment and **do** block | the implicit access is enumerated (LO-2, IW-1), proved acyclic (§16.2.7), published (`implicitAssignmentReferenceFunctions[]`) and tested (T-107b); no explicit lock is added, consistent with CCA §37 |
| 49 | "every mint is evidenced" (XF-15) was false for a signature produced before the mint transaction committed and then rolled back | XF-16 commit-before-sign, CB-23, T-171d |
| 50 | the round-3 signer returned `M7011` from the liveness helper for a retired backend, contradicting XF-14's single indistinguishable `M7013` | the helper's `M7011` is caught inside the signer and re-raised as `M7013` |
| 51 | registration probes (`c_register_storage_backend_v1`, `…_profile_v1`, `…_retention_policy_v1`, `…_merchant_vocabulary_v1`, `…_manifest_v1`) took `FOR UPDATE` on immutable rows, conflicting with every class-10 `FOR SHARE` and every foreign-key `FOR KEY SHARE` for no benefit | `FOR SHARE` (LG-4) |
| 52 | T-169 predicted a `23505` for concurrent mints that the function could not produce once the intent was locked; T-109 claimed no participant operation blocks behind a rotation, false for SO-2 behind a retirement; T-77 said `96` functions; IMP-06 said `eight` two-backend cases while §25.22 said `9` and listed ten; §26.1's distribution was not reproducible | each corrected against the actual SQL or regenerated by rule |
| 53 | a design considered for signer routing let the signer choose among the backend's live profiles itself, which would have placed a capability decision in the one process whose fidelity the database cannot see | rejected before drafting: the database resolves and records the signing profile after the liveness lock; the signer only looks up the credential it is told to use and refuses if absent (XC-7) |
| 54 | a design considered for AUD-02 serialized every `c_*` transaction behind a PostgreSQL advisory lock. Any login role can take the same advisory key (an availability attack on rotation), the mutex would be invisible to the catalog verifier, and the brief prefers a consistent order | rejected before drafting: deadlock freedom follows from LG-4, and the two genuinely serial races use row locks on M7 rows no login role can touch (RC-23) |

### A.2.4 Defects found during the round-5 re-derivation

The brief required the lock graph to be re-derived under the conservative queue rule and re-audited for every retirement race and all five multi-backend batches, and the replay contract to be made exact. The re-derivation found the following beyond the two audited findings. #55–#60 are defects fixed in this candidate; #61–#63 are designs considered and rejected.

| # | Defect found | Fix |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 55 | **A second three-way cycle of the audited kind, through sessions.** `r_record_erasure_request_v1` holds the session `FOR SHARE` (P1) and then takes `FOR KEY SHARE` on the assignment (P3); SO-1/2/3 hold the assignment and then request the session `FOR SHARE`; a revocation *waiting* for `FOR UPDATE` on the session sits between them. Under the conservative PG-1 this is a cycle with **one** assignment and one session | the revocation no longer waits: insert-first, `NOWAIT` quiescence probe, RV-1…RV-5 (LG-10; §16.2.8 Corollary 2; RC-27; T-191) |
| 56 | **A cycle between two batch schedulers.** Their P3 loops were ordered by `backendSha256`, so two batches could take assignment `FOR KEY SHARE` locks in opposite orders; A1 withdrawals waiting on both assignments make the queue edges that close it | LG-8: P3 loops ordered by `"assignmentId"` (§16.2.8 Corollary 3; RC-28; T-192) |
| 57 | Redaction's replay check ran only before the assignment lock, so a concurrent duplicate failed `23505` exactly as the audited purge replay did | RM-1 post-lock re-read in both mechanisms (RC-29; T-61 (c)) |
| 58 | `w_execute_row_purge_v1` read its authorization `STRICT` before the assignment lock; a concurrent residue-prohibited purge committing between its two reads surfaced as `P0002` instead of a typed outcome | non-`STRICT` read mapped to `EXECUTION_ABSENT` (RM-4) |
| 59 | The round-4 §16.2.4 argument that A1/A2 appear only at the end of an M7 wait chain relied on PG-1's no-queueing clause: an IW-1 taker can queue behind an A1 withdrawal that waits on another IW-1 holder | re-derived from PA-1…PA-4 without the clause; IW-1 targets now include other IW-1 holders (table IW, LV-11) |
| 60 | T-173 order 2, T-176's third sub-case, T-182 (b), T-185, T-186 and T-187 (c), (d) asserted a retirement that **waits** (or fails at `lock_timeout`), which the round-5 design no longer permits | each re-stated with `M7014` and the re-run's outcome |
| 61 | *Considered:* keep waiting retirements and add ascending order between class 10 and class 1 for work transactions | rejected: SO-2 must take the assignment first (CCA §30) and the liveness lock after it, while schedulers necessarily hold class 10 before their P3 assignment reference; no single order serves both, and the cycle needs only one waiter |
| 62 | *Considered:* make work transactions take the backend with `FOR KEY SHARE` and give non-last profile retirements `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, so credential rotation would not compete with work | rejected for this round: it changes the RC-25 / XF-17 serialization accepted in round 4 and moves the signer's routing proof onto profile rows; the retirement-progress cost is recorded instead (M7-R-16) |
| 63 | *Considered:* a hidden replay marker for residue-prohibited purges so a retry could return the original count | rejected, as the brief requires: it would be residue under JBA §16.6.1 Case 2 (RM-5) |

| # | Check | Result |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 1 | authority conflicts | 9 found and resolved explicitly by precedence in §4.2 (AC-01…AC-09; AC-08 and AC-09 are new and arise from AUD-04 and AUD-01). None resolved silently |
| 2 | unauthorized new semantics | None introduced in consent, A1, A2, B or C. §4 of the brief honoured: no second consent algorithm, no SQL re-implementation of the A1 predicate, sealed CCA unchanged, M7-R-01 kept explicit |

| 4 | undefined roles / functions | None: **7** roles, **110** functions, **8** transaction owners, all defined; every EXECUTE grant is derived by capability and re-verified by exact-set comparison. All three numbers are derived per §19.14.1, not carried forward |
| 5a | impossible PostgreSQL DDL, round 2 | Three further checks: (a) `extract(epoch FROM interval)` is IMMUTABLE and safe inside `i_backend_digest`, while `interval` itself is not directly hashable, so the digest uses the numeric seconds; (b) a composite FK onto `(id, encoderGeneration)` requires that UNIQUE on `m7_storage_profile`, which is added, and its `MATCH SIMPLE` behaviour over the NULL redacted case is relied on deliberately; (c) the three `boundPolicyVersion` FKs each need a UNIQUE on the referenced side — added on the intent, the execution and the finding — and `ON CONFLICT` is not used on any of them |
| 5 | impossible PostgreSQL DDL | The four defects fixed in the prior round are retained as fixed (`statement_timeout` out of `proconfig`; `COALESCE` is syntax, not `pg_catalog.coalesce`; self-referential supersession FKs use `NO ACTION`; the one-active rule needs an expression-based partial unique index). **Three new ones found and fixed:** (a) a partial unique index cannot be an `ON CONFLICT` arbiter unless the predicate is restated, so `i_enqueue_delete` spells out `WHERE "state" IN ('PENDING','LEASED')`; (b) `timestamptz + interval` is STABLE and cannot appear in a CHECK, so every deadline CHECK compares two stored `timestamptz` columns or an interval difference; (c) a composite FK requires a matching UNIQUE on the referenced side, so `m7_storage_profile(id, backendSha256)`, `m7_evidence_upload_intent(id, backendSha256)`, `m7_canonical_generation(uploadIntentId, leaseEpoch, backendSha256)` and `m7_storage_outbox(id, backendSha256)` each carry one |
| 6 | SQL privilege bypasses | Login roles hold **no** table or column privilege; every write path also requires owner context plus the function's write path (T-02); `c_*` has no login grantee (T-08b, T-137) |
| 7 | `SECURITY DEFINER` shadowing / `search_path` | `pg_catalog, pg_temp` with `pg_temp` last, full qualification (including `pg_catalog.starts_with`, newly security-relevant), `PUBLIC` EXECUTE revoked, exact-set catalog verified |
| 8 | consent capability detachment | No M7 value carries consent; the session capability carries no consent material and authorizes nothing (§8.3) |
| 9 | participant substitution | Closed against every non-owner actor lacking the live session secret (M7-I09); authentication boundary recorded as M7-R-02 |
| 10 | uploader capability replay | One-use by terminal state plus `UNIQUE(uploadIntentId)`/`UNIQUE(observationId)`/`UNIQUE(uploadIntentId, acceptedLeaseEpoch)`; the presigned-URL limitation is bounded to staging on one backend (M7-R-06) **and to the staging write fence**, after which a late `PUT` cannot land at all (§11.7) |
| 11 | object-key substitution | No function accepts a key; the staging key is generated at issuance, canonical keys at claim, and both are prefix-verified against the **bound** backend (M7-I24, M7-I88) |
| 12 | storage race windows | **29** races and **24** crash boundaries enumerated with serialization points (§16.3, §17.3), each identifier carrying exactly one meaning (§16.3.1). Round 5 appends RC-26…RC-29 (the three conservative-queueing schedules and the concurrent row-mechanism duplicate) and CB-24 (a row mechanism whose response is lost). Round 4 appends RC-22…RC-25 (activation vs retirement, concurrent activations, a mint waiting across expiry, a mint during credential rotation) and CB-23 (a mint that did not commit is never signed). Round-3 state: RC-17 (two claims racing to allocate a generation) and RC-18 (observation while a new epoch claims) keep their round-1 meanings; RC-19 (stale `PUT` versus its own key's deletion), RC-20 (policy rotation versus an in-flight effect) and RC-21 (retirement versus the creation of backend-scoped work, **rewritten** onto the two-sided lock) are the round-2 races re-identified; CB-19…CB-22 cover grant expiry, near-expiry acceptance, grant/generation atomicity and a lost mint response. Both counts are derived per §19.14.1 |
| 13 | transaction crash windows | Object-first/DB-second creation plus outbox confirmation-on-absence; no half-committed claim is representable (CB-09); a rotation is one transaction (CB-16) |
| 14 | stale worker completion | Epoch fencing on intents and outbox rows, per-generation external keys, **and a per-generation immutable authorization envelope with a persisted fence**, so the stale epoch loses the ability to *create* its key and not merely to have it adopted (M7-I93, M7-I106…I110, M7-I118). Round 3 withdrew the round-2 claim that only one capability was ever *signed* — that is unobservable from PostgreSQL (§11.7.0) — and replaced it with the claim that no envelope M7 can mint is *wider*, which is what the fence arithmetic actually needs. The provider half is an ACL fact (M7-I107 / M7-R-09) and the signer half is capability topology (M7-I119 / M7-R-12, class **E-E**); both are carried honestly rather than claimed as enforced |
| 15 | deletion bypass | Every basis recomputed in the database; authority and execution separated; completion must be evidenced **on the bound backend**; deadlines derived, not supplied (M7-I46…I53, I88, I99…I101) |
| 16 | correction cycles / conflicts | Single successor + strictly increasing sequence + terminal retraction; competing corrections fail explicitly rather than being merged |
| 17 | "latest wins" residue | Searched for and absent, including in the new generation model: a key is written once by one epoch and adopted only if that epoch was current (GF-9). The one ordered read (`i_withdrawal_event`) selects among at most one row and is documented; `i_require_routable_profile`'s `ORDER BY credentialGeneration DESC` selects a *credential*, never a fact, and is constrained to one backend — and §11.8 now makes the profile it selects a **recorded** execution fact rather than an implicit one. Re-checked in round 2: no timing value, no deadline and no drain predicate is resolved "from the current control plane" any more (DL-5, §11.9) |
| 18 | hidden candidate / denominator semantics | Candidates and generations classified separately from canonical facts; `0` denominator effects; existence of a root is explicitly not an occurrence claim |

| 21 | machine-authority selector invention | Not asserted, not inferred, not rotated; §24 states what a future rotation must prove, now including MA-9…MA-12 |

| **24** | **lock graph and transaction owners** *(new in round 4)* | Re-derived from the SQL rather than from the round-3 prose: every definer function has a row in §16.2.6; every implicit wait (foreign keys, non-key updates, deletes, unique insertions) is in §16.2.7; LG-THEOREM is proved from those tables under stated PostgreSQL premises. Defects found by this check and fixed: the three audited inversions (signer, classification, activation), five loop functions interleaving class 10 with ordinary locks, an unordered multi-backend acquisition in the purge, a vocabulary registration that could never succeed, a requeue guard that could never pass, an SLA-assertion job with unordered unique insertions, and a T-107 claim contradicted by five foreign keys (A.2.3). The owner model now has eight rows, TO-8 included, and §18.6 is checked against it (T-189) |
| **25** | **count provenance** *(new in round 4)* | Every number displayed in §19.14, §25.22, §26.1 and §27.6 was produced by a rule over the final text; round 3's subtotal row that summed to 40, its §26.1 distribution (not reproducible by any rule over its own §26), T-77's `96` and IMP-06's `eight` were stale and are replaced (§19.14.1) |
| **26** | **environmental premises** *(new in round 5)* | Every statement about PostgreSQL behaviour used by a proof was checked for whether PostgreSQL guarantees it or merely often exhibits it. One was only the latter — round 4's PG-1 no-queueing clause — and it was replaced by a conservative premise; the design was then changed (LG-8, LG-10) until the proof held without it, and the re-derivation found two further cycles (A.2.4 #55, #56). The remaining premises (conflict matrix, implicit lock modes, `NOWAIT` leaving no waiter) are named in PG-1…PG-3 and tested by T-188 |
| **23** | **external capability minting boundary** *(new in round 3)* | Searched for every path by which an actor inside M7's own capability topology could obtain a **wider** write authorization than a generation's envelope, and for every place a database object is credited with fencing something produced outside the database. Findings: the round-2 XF-9 and theorem step (2) (fixed, §11.7.0); a worker-reachable signer credential (fixed, XC-3/XC-5); an envelope FK missing two components (fixed, A.2.2 #33). Remaining: the signer's own fidelity, which no database object or provider ACL reaches — recorded as M7-I119 (**E-E**), M7-R-12, IMP-18 and T-171b, **not** as a closed claim |

## A.4 Author-flagged judgement calls for the auditor's attention

These are decisions, not defects, and each is argued in place.

| # | Decision | Where argued |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| J-1 | Treating upload-intent issuance (SO-2) as consent-conditioned under the **existing** evidence policy, rather than creating a third policy | §9.2, AC-07 |
| J-2 | Reading the A1 `WITHDRAWN` event as the RT-17 **deletion trigger** while never reading consent for authorization | §15.2, AC-06, `i_withdrawal_event` |
| J-3 | Granting the M7 owner `UPDATE("id")` on `public.experiment_assignment`, solely so `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` is permitted, with the A1 append-only trigger still rejecting every actual update | §18.2, §19.2 |
| J-4 | Seven new C-class transaction owners (TO-2…TO-8), one of which (the row mechanisms, TO-5) takes an explicit lock on `experiment_assignment` and one of which (the capability signer, TO-8) is its own process — permitted only via an accepted authority artifact under CCA §33 class C | §16.2.3, §18.6, LO-1 |
| J-5 | A governed merchant vocabulary instead of either a fixed list or free text, plus RP-5 ref stability as a rotation obligation | §13.4, §9.5, MA-4 |
| J-6 | Requiring PostgreSQL ≥ 15 | §19.1, IA-08 |
| J-7 | Issuing **no** evidence download URLs in V1.1, deferring verifier reads to C1S — and requiring that a future reader resolve bytes through the artifact's own profile | §11.5, C1-OB-6 |
| J-8 | **Two** levels of storage identity (backend and profile) rather than one. A single level would force a credential rotation to look like a backend rotation, stranding historical objects; the split is what makes credential rotation transparent and backend rotation honest | §11.1.2, §11.1.3 |
| J-9 | Paying one extra canonical object per lease expiry to obtain external fencing, instead of reusing a single key with read-back | §11.6.3, M7-R-08 |
| J-10 | **Draining** rather than migrating a decommissioned backend, and granting no migration path at all | §11.4, M7-R-07 |
| J-11 | Recording `budgetSatisfied = false` and proceeding, rather than refusing to schedule a late deletion | §15.3, T-129b |
| J-12 | Six manifest-driven expectation tables inside the database, rather than an external-only comparison. The cost is six control-plane tables; the benefit is that the check runs **in** the database the guarantees live in, and can gate writes (IMP-07) | §19.5, §19.13.1 |
| J-13 | Keeping `i_assert_control_plane` strict on replay paths (RP-6), accepting that a deployment mid-rotation cannot serve replays, in exchange for no drifted deployment ever writing | §9.5.1 RP-6, §23.6 |
| **J-14** | Requiring SP-9 — a provider-enforced bound `W` on accepted-to-visible write time — as a **capability requirement with a declared value**, rather than assuming signature expiry alone fences a write. This is the round-2 brief's *"request that starts near capability expiry and completes later"*. It makes M7 unusable on a provider that cannot bound it, and the author judges that correct: without such a bound, no proof of absence is completable | §11.2 SP-9, §11.7.2, IMP-15, M7-R-09 |
| **J-15** | Making `G` (the grant TTL), not the lease, the worker's real budget for the canonical write. A stalled write cannot be rescued by extending the capability; it must be reclaimed at a new epoch. The cost is one more bounded extra object | §11.7.2, XF-9, M7-R-11 |
| **J-16** | Keeping the write-grant **envelope** and the **mint record** in the database while keeping the signature out of both. The rows fix *what any capability for this key may authorize* and record *that one was issued, with which envelope digest*; storing the signature would add an exfiltration class and would still not bound how many were signed (§11.7.0) | §11.7.3 XF-8, XF-15, §20.3 |
| **J-17** | Recording the executing profile **per generation** rather than per intent or per submission. A single intent can be executed by two different profiles across two epochs, and only the generation is granular enough to be true about both | §11.8.2, T-118b |
| **J-18** | Letting `issuanceProfileId` and `executingProfileId` differ **freely**, with no constraint relating them. Any relation between them would re-introduce the round-2 defect in a weaker form | §11.8.3 EP-2, T-145 |
| **J-19** | Giving housekeeping outbox families (`UPLOAD_INTENT`, `RECONCILIATION_RUN`) their own explicitly named bound policy instead of exempting them to the active manifest. The brief permits an explicit source; it does not permit a silent one | §15.11.6 DL-5 |
| **J-20** | Representing a post-budget requeue as **recovery after an SLA failure** — durable failure row, monotone attempt counter, `withinCompletionBudget = false` on the eventual completion — rather than refusing the requeue. Refusing it would leave bytes in place to protect a metric, which is the same error §15.11.2's J-11 rejects | §15.11.6 DL-6…DL-8, T-154 |
| **J-21** | Adding classes 6 and 7 (evidenced absence of **every** key M7 wrote) to the drain predicate, making retirement strictly harder than either previous definition. The alternative was to keep a sentence the implementation did not support | §11.9.2, T-161, T-162 |
| **J-22** | Publishing the XF-THEOREM as an explicit proof with named premises, including the premises PostgreSQL cannot check. A proof whose assumptions are visible can be audited; a claim of enforcement cannot | §11.7.5, §26.1, §29 |
| **J-23** | **Withdrawing the token-uniqueness claim outright rather than trying to rescue it.** A `UNIQUE(grantId)` on the mint table would have let the round-2 wording stand, and would have been false in exactly the same way while also breaking CB-22 recovery. The author judges that a claim the enforcing layer cannot reach must be *replaced*, not shored up | §11.7.0, A.2.2 #32 |
| **J-24** | **Allowing an identical re-mint (case D) rather than refusing it.** Refusing would make a lost mint response unrecoverable and push a worker toward obtaining a capability out of band — the very behaviour the finding is about. Safety is placed in envelope *immutability* (XF-11) and in `mintSeq` *visibility* (XF-15), not in a count | §11.7.6 case D, T-169, CB-22 |
| **J-25** | **A separate database role and a separate module for the signer, at the cost of a seventh role and a sixth credential.** The alternative — keeping minting in the worker and relying on a runbook — is what round 2 did, and it is why the defect was reachable without any out-of-band credential. The cost is real; the author judges the separation is the only part of this an auditor can check in the catalog | §11.7.3 XF-13, §18.2, IA-14, IMP-18 |
| **J-26** | **Classifying the signer half as E-E and saying so in five places** (§11.7.4, §11.7.7, M7-I119, M7-R-12, §29) rather than describing the signer function's SQL and letting a reader infer enforcement. `M7V11R3-AUD-01` is precisely what happens when a layer is credited with more than it does | §11.7.4, §26.1 |
| **J-27** | **Overloading the `m7_storage_backend` row as lock class 10 instead of creating a liveness table**, and stating the class-0 exception explicitly. The row is immutable apart from retirement, so a `FOR SHARE` holder blocks only on the event the lock exists for; a dedicated table would add a relation, a PK, a FK and three triggers holding no data | §16.2.2, §11.10.3 BL-1, A.2.2 #38 |
| **J-28** | *(withdrawn in round 4 — see J-31)* **Applying BL-2 to *every* backend-scoped write, including integrity findings that cannot keep a backend non-drained (WC-14).** A rule with an exception list is a rule someone will extend wrongly; a uniform rule is source-checkable in both directions (T-180). The cost is a redundant `FOR SHARE` on two functions | §11.10.4, BL-2, T-180 |
| **J-29** | **Making `c_retire_storage_backend_v1`'s RT-2 refusal `55000` rather than `M7009`, and checking it before the drain predicate.** An auditor reading a failure must be able to tell "this backend still holds bytes" from "this backend is the one the system is currently using"; collapsing them into the drain predicate would hide a coherence defect inside a quiescence report | §11.10.2 RT-2, T-172 |
| **J-30** | **Treating the referential-integrity `FOR KEY SHARE` on `experiment_assignment` as enumerated implicit access rather than a direct assignment lock under CCA §37, instead of removing the five foreign keys or adding explicit locks.** Removing the keys would weaken integrity proofs; explicit locks would be the direct access CCA §37 reserves for the CCA engine. The implicit wait is proved to close no cycle and is tested | §16.2.3 LO-2, §16.2.7 IW-1, T-107b |
| **J-31** | **Withdrawing J-28's uniform liveness rule.** A lock on every backend-scoped write was source-checkable but was not what BL-SAFE requires, and it added lock-graph edges and one retired-backend exception. The derived set is equally source-checkable (T-180) and has no exception | §11.10.3, §11.10.4, NW-1…NW-6 |
| **J-32** | **Row mechanisms refuse rather than wait on a busy row after the assignment lock.** It makes TO-5 a never-waiting state after its assignment lock (N2) and costs retries under contention (M7-R-15) | §16.2.5 LG-5, LG-6 |
| **J-33** | **Resolving the signing profile in the database, preferring the generation's executing profile**, rather than always the newest live credential. Continuity with the profile the generation already runs under avoids a credential switch mid-pipeline; the fallback exists only so a completed rotation does not strand live grants | §11.7.3 XF-17, `i_signing_profile` |
| **J-34** | **Stating PostgreSQL row-lock semantics as premises of the no-deadlock theorem**, tested on the deployed version, rather than a proof that pretends to be version-independent. *Round 5:* the premises are now the weakest ones certainly true; the queueing policy for compatible requests is observed and recorded by T-188 (i) but no longer assumed | §16.2.5 PG-1…PG-3, T-188, M7-R-14 |
| **J-35** | **Non-waiting retirements (`NOWAIT` + governed retry) rather than any mechanism that lets a retirement win against work.** The auditor's proposed direction was evaluated and adopted: it removes the only exclusive waiter on the backend row, keeps the fail-closed direction, and costs retirement progress under sustained load (M7-R-16). The author judges progress-by-retry correct for an operation that is never urgent on a timescale of seconds | §11.10.8, LG-10, T-190, T-193 |
| **J-36** | **An insert-first revocation with a `NOWAIT` quiescence probe, and a two-valued result**, rather than a waiting revocation or a revocation that aborts when busy. The first is the cycle of A.2.4 #55; the second could be starved by the very session being revoked. Recording the revocation first makes it effective immediately for new validations, and `QUIESCENT` restores the strong guarantee before the module reports completion | §8.2 RV-1…RV-5, T-191 |
| **J-37** | **Changing `s_revoke_participant_session_v1` to `RETURNS text`** — the only function signature change in round 5. The argument list, EXECUTE grantee and write path are unchanged; the manifest's function expectation set carries the new definition | §19.11.3 |
| **J-38** | **`EXECUTION_ABSENT` shared by "purged without residue" and "never existed"**, deliberately indistinguishable, rather than a typed "already purged" answer. Any distinguishing response would be a residue channel | §15.7.1 RM-4, RM-5, M7-R-17 |
